headline_en: Sylhet migrant killed by co-worker in Middle East, another dies in accident
summary_en: Two migrants from Bishwanath upazila, Sylhet, died in the Middle East just after Eid: Sabul Mia (39) died in a road accident in Muscat, Oman, when the driver of their car fell asleep, and Foyzul Haque (55) was stabbed to death at his workplace in Abu Dhabi, UAE, reportedly by two Bangladeshi co-workers who were arrested. Families learned via contacts abroad; Sabul's body was in a morgue with repatriation under discussion, while there was no progress on bringing Foyzul's body home.

facts.statement: Sabul Mia (39), of Hasnaji village, Daulatpur union, Bishwanath upazila, Sylhet, died on the morning of Wednesday (about 2 April 2025) in a road accident in the Amla-Ibri (আমলা-ইবরি) area of Muscat, Oman, while he and three others were being driven to work; the driver suddenly fell asleep, the car went out of control and Sabul and two others died on the spot.

Sabul Mia had been working in Oman for about 9 years, had visited Bangladesh twice, returned to Oman last December after about two and a half months of leave, and was due to return home for good in one more year. He leaves a son aged two and a half.
Sabul Mia's family in Bishwanath, Sylhet learned of his death in Oman on Wednesday (about 2 April 2025) through a man from their area who lives in Oman.

As of about 4 April 2025, Sabul Mia's body was kept in the morgue of a local hospital in Muscat, Oman; detailed discussions on bringing the body home were under way and the family hoped it could be brought to Bangladesh within the following week.

Foyzul Haque (55), of Bhurki village, Lamakazi union, Bishwanath upazila, Sylhet, was stabbed to death around midday on Tuesday (about 1 April 2025) at his workplace in the Shamkha (শামখা) area of Abu Dhabi, UAE; the family initially learned that two Bangladeshi co-workers stabbed him, and they were arrested by UAE police.
Foyzul Haque's family learned of his death in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday evening (about 2 April 2025) through one of his co-workers, because nobody from their area lives in that country.

As of about 4 April 2025, Foyzul Haque's family said there had been no real progress on bringing his body home from Abu Dhabi, UAE. He had returned to Abu Dhabi about three months earlier after leave in Bangladesh, and leaves a wife, a son and a daughter.

headline_en: Bangladeshi sent back from India over alleged anti-India remarks
summary_en: Indian authorities cancelled the visa of Md. Azadur Rahman of Magura and sent him back to Bangladesh through Changrabandha immigration, Cooch Behar, on 25 March 2025, after he allegedly made offensive remarks about India during a dispute with a taxi driver. Local residents protested after the incident spread on Facebook live; police rescued him, and immigration cancelled his visa after consulting the Kolkata FRRO.

facts.statement: On Tuesday 25 March 2025, Md. Azadur Rahman, from Magura district, Bangladesh, had his Indian visa cancelled and was sent back to Bangladesh from the Changrabandha immigration point in Cooch Behar, West Bengal, accused of making anti-India remarks.
facts.source_in_article: Mekhliganj block police officer Ashish P Subba; Indian media

facts.statement: Azadur Rahman's son studies in Kurseong, Darjeeling, India; Azadur had planned to return to Bangladesh with his son after the son's exams.

According to Indian paper Uttarbanga Sambad citing witnesses, Azadur argued with a driver while hiring a car at the taxi stand near the Changrabandha immigration checkpost, behaved badly with several people and made very offensive comments about India; drivers refused to take him, people streamed it live on Facebook, and residents surrounded and protested against him at Changrabandha VIP crossing. Exactly what he said about India was not known.

Mekhliganj police station rescued Azadur Rahman as the situation heated up, took him to the police station and then brought him back to the Changrabandha immigration checkpost; he admitted his mistake before the crowd but did not answer journalists.

An official of the Changrabandha international immigration office said Azadur Rahman's visa was cancelled after talking with the Kolkata FRRO (Foreigners Regional Registration Office), and he was then sent back to Bangladesh.

Early election in Germany: how hard will it be for Bangladeshi migrants?
summary_en: A Bangladeshi reader writing from Hamburg reports that Germany is heading for an early election, possibly on 23 February 2025, with the far-right AfD polling 18 percent. An AfD campaigner told him the party welcomes migrants with legal work status but wants rules on migration; the writer concludes asylum seekers without work authorisation would find it hard if AfD came to power, while most Bangladeshis in Germany work legally and may not be much affected.

facts.statement: As of December 2024, Germany's early national election could be held on 23 February 2025, according to German parliament sources quoted by news agencies DPA and AFP, after Chancellor Olaf Scholz's coalition broke up when he dismissed FDP finance minister Christian Lindner.
facts.source_in_article: DPA and AFP citing parliament sources

facts.statement: A Der Spiegel election research group poll (as of December 2024) gave CDU 33 percent, the far-right AfD 18 percent, SPD 16 percent, Greens 12 percent and FDP 3 percent support.

Many Bangladeshis and other migrants living in Germany fear that if the far-right AfD (Alternative for Germany, founded 2013) comes to power, living in Germany would become harder for migrants and asylum seekers.

An AfD campaigner in Hamburg told the Bangladeshi writer that the party welcomes migrants who have legal work status and wants them to play a bigger role in Germany's future, but wants to bring migrants within a set of rules.

The writer's reading is that if AfD comes to power, it would be truly hard for asylum-seeker migrants without legal work status to stay in Germany, and the party would not support uncontrolled mass migration.
After the fall of the Assad government, the German government had already stopped (processing) applications from Syrian asylum seekers, as of December 2024.
According to the writer, most Bangladeshis currently in Germany work legally, and he did not think an AfD government would cause them much harm.
Prothom Alo's Durporobash (diaspora) section accepts writing, travel stories, videos and photos at dp@prothomalo.com.

headline_en: Bangladeshi credit card use now highest in the US instead of India
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data show that after July 2024 the United States overtook India as the top country for Bangladeshi credit card spending abroad, with about BDT 77 crore spent there in September 2024. Bankers attribute the fall in India (from BDT 92 crore in June to 51 crore) to India restricting visas for Bangladeshis to emergency medical cases since July/August; spending rose in Thailand and Malaysia as alternative travel destinations.

facts.statement: Bankers said that from July 2024 (the article also says after the political change in August) India tightened visas for Bangladeshis and now limits tourist and other visas, apart from emergency medical visas, so Bangladeshi travel to India fell significantly.
In September 2024 Bangladeshis spent about BDT 77 crore by credit card in the United States, the highest of any foreign country, and about 18 percent of all Bangladeshi credit card spending abroad.
Bangladeshi credit card spending in India was BDT 51 crore in September 2024 and the same in August 2024, down from a high of BDT 92 crore in June 2024 before the July student movement, roughly half.
Total Bangladeshi credit card spending abroad was about BDT 421 crore in September 2024, up from BDT 373 crore in August, an increase of BDT 48 crore or about 13 percent.

Bangladeshi credit card spending in Thailand rose from BDT 33 crore in August 2024 to BDT 42 crore in September 2024 (up 9 crore, about 27.25 percent); in Malaysia and the Netherlands it rose by BDT 5 crore each over the same month. Bankers said Thailand and Malaysia had become main travel destinations after India tightened visas.

Domestic credit card spending in Bangladesh was BDT 2,668 crore in September 2024 vs BDT 2,332 crore in August (up 336 crore, 14.40 percent). The report covers 44 card-issuing banks and 1 financial institution.
Abroad, Bangladeshis spent most by credit card at department stores (BDT 116 crore in September 2024) and second most at retail outlet services (BDT 74 crore), both up from August.

headline_en: Saudi Arabia asks about progress in renewing passports of Rohingyas who went there on Bangladeshi passports
summary_en: On 12 May 2024 Saudi Deputy Interior Minister Naser bin Abdul Aziz Al-Dawood met Bangladesh Home Minister Asaduzzaman Khan in Dhaka and asked about progress in renewing Bangladeshi passports held by Rohingyas who went to Saudi Arabia in 1973-74 (about 69,000 by the Saudi count). The home minister said they will not be sent back to Bangladesh but their passports must be renewed under a signed MoU, keeping passport details unchanged; he noted Saudi law deports people without valid papers.

facts.statement: Saudi Deputy Interior Minister Naser bin Abdul Aziz Al-Dawood, at a bilateral meeting with Bangladesh Home Minister Asaduzzaman Khan at a Dhaka hotel on Sunday 12 May 2024, asked about progress in renewing the passports of Rohingyas who went to Saudi Arabia on Bangladeshi passports in 1973-74.

The Saudi side told Bangladesh that about 69,000 Rohingyas went to Saudi Arabia (on Bangladeshi passports) in 1973-74; Bangladesh's home minister said the exact number was unknown to Bangladesh and could be more or less.

Bangladesh's home minister said Rohingyas living in Saudi Arabia (on Bangladeshi passports) will not be sent back to Bangladesh, but their passports must be renewed, and a memorandum of understanding on this has been signed with Saudi Arabia; the passports will be renewed with their information unchanged.
Under Saudi government law, people without valid papers are sent back (deported).

The Saudi deputy minister came to check whether Bangladesh was moving slowly, facing problems or had loopholes in renewing Rohingyas' passports; the two sides also discussed cooperation to build BGB and police capacity, and Saudi Arabia stressed safe repatriation of Rohingyas to Myanmar as soon as possible.

headline_en: Father who returned from abroad denies us as his children
summary_en: In a legal advice column, a migrant's child writes that their father worked abroad for about 22 years, sending BDT 20,000 a month and beating their mother on each home visit, then returned for good in 2023, stopped paying household costs, abuses the mother and disowns the children. Barrister Miti Sanjana of the Supreme Court explains that this is domestic violence under the Domestic Violence (Prevention and Protection) Act 2010 and lists the remedies and where to apply.

facts.statement: A letter writer (anonymous) said their father went abroad after marrying about 22 years ago, came home every three years for three months, sent BDT 20,000 a month, and beat their mother on each visit; after returning home for good in 2023 he stopped paying the family's expenses, abuses and beats the mother daily, wants a divorce, denies the children as his, and now wants to file a case against the mother and brother.

Under Bangladesh's Domestic Violence (Prevention and Protection) Act 2010, domestic violence means physical, mental or sexual abuse or financial harm by a family member against a woman or child in the family; the Act made domestic violence an offence for the first time and rules under it have been framed. Withholding maintenance (financial deprivation) is covered.
facts.source_in_article: Barrister Miti Sanjana, Supreme Court lawyer

facts.statement: A woman facing domestic violence in Bangladesh can, under the 2010 Act, seek remedies, medical treatment, services from an enforcement officer, and, where applicable, free legal advice and aid under the Legal Aid Act 2000.

An application under the Domestic Violence Act 2010 can be made by the victim or on her behalf by an enforcement officer, service provider or any other person; the court sets a hearing date within seven days of receiving it. The woman can apply for protection to the officer-in-charge of any police station, a women affairs officer, or directly to the court.

Remedies under the Domestic Violence Act 2010: interim protection order (section 13, can be ex parte); protection order after hearing both sides; residence order (section 15, barring the abuser from the home, stopping eviction, arranging safe shelter with consent, bond with or without surety); compensation/maintenance order (section 16, one-off or monthly maintenance for the woman and child at their accustomed standard of living); safe custody order for the child (section 17).

Offences under the Domestic Violence Act 2010 are cognisable, bailable and compoundable; punishment is in section 30, but under section 31 the court may instead order community service for a set period. Separately, Penal Code section 323 punishes voluntarily causing hurt with up to one year in jail or a BDT 1,000 fine or both.

headline_en: How to prepare for higher study abroad: the steps
summary_en: A general guide for Bangladeshi students planning higher study abroad, covering decision and planning (at least a year ahead), language tests (IELTS, TOEFL and others), researching courses and universities, applying to several universities, funding and scholarships, the student visa process, accommodation, and travel preparation.

facts.statement: Going abroad for higher study takes at least a year of well-planned activity; seminars, workshops and counselling on careers and study abroad during the bachelor's can help, but the student must decide.

Most universities in developed countries require proof of English; most accept academic IELTS or TOEFL. Some well-known European universities require other languages, chiefly Mandarin Chinese, German, French, Arabic and Japanese.
The article names the British Council, IDP and the Institute of Modern Languages at Dhaka University as the best places in Bangladesh to sit tests and get language proficiency certificates.

When researching, check course content, research scope, campus life, job prospects, tuition costs and scholarships; Facebook groups on higher study, alumni and teachers are useful sources; shortlist two or three destinations and compare them.

Applicants with a good CGPA apply to several universities, built around their final-year thesis or project paper; follow each university's admission instructions exactly. Some want only digital copies of documents, others also want physical copies by post; information must be consistent across all certificates.

Tuition fees are very high in the United States, Canada, Australia, the United Kingdom and Singapore; part-time work alone cannot cover study costs, and international students are allowed only a limited number of work hours per week.

According to the article, public universities in Norway, Germany and China give degrees free to all international students regardless of nationality, but living costs are high, so scholarships are the best funding route. Before going, a bank balance must be shown to cover all living costs in that country.

In EU countries short language courses are sometimes allowed on a tourist visa, but almost all courses longer than three months need a student visa. Usually an offer letter from a university is needed before applying; after paying the required admission fee, the institution provides the documents needed for the student visa application. Visa processes differ by country.

Students often face problems arranging housing abroad, so it is best to fix accommodation before leaving; options are university-provided housing (sometimes with scholarships), student dormitories (may share kitchen or bathroom), sharing with local residents (sublet), or a pricier apartment, often shared.

Book flights as early as possible to save money, check cancellation and change policies, arrive well before classes start, follow the airline's baggage limits (extra baggage costs more), and pack student ID, passport and essential medicines.

headline_en: Qatar Bondhushava gives Eid gifts to migrants
summary_en: On 5 April 2024 Qatar Bondhushava, the Qatar chapter of Prothom Alo's readers' club, gave Eid food packages to 65 Bangladeshi migrants in Qatar who were jobless and looking for new work, and clothes to 15 people, with support from local businesses including Al Zaman Cleaning, J&Rap Trading and New Space Hospitality.

facts.statement: Many Bangladeshi migrants in Qatar were currently jobless and looking for new work, according to Qatar Bondhushava; on 5 April 2024 it gave Eid food packages to 65 such migrants and clothes to 15 people under the 'Eid of compassion' (সহমর্মিতার ঈদ) programme called by Bondhushava's national governing body.

Qatar Bondhushava (Prothom Alo readers' club, Qatar chapter) said it would keep working to support Bangladeshi expatriates in Qatar; the April 2024 distribution was supported by expatriates, social figures and the businesses Al Zaman Cleaning (owner Sabrina Afroz), J&Rap Trading and New Space Hospitality (Mohammad Bayezid).

headline_en: Bangladeshis fifth in setting up second homes in Malaysia
summary_en: As of 31 January 2024, 3,604 Bangladeshis held Malaysia My Second Home (MM2H) passes, fifth after China, Australia, South Korea and Japan, according to Malaysia's tourism minister in parliament as reported by Malay Mail. The programme was restructured in December 2023 into Platinum, Gold and Silver tiers with fixed-deposit requirements of 5 million, 2 million and 500,000 ringgit, a minimum age of 30 and a 60-day annual stay requirement. The article notes allegations that laundered money funds such second homes.

facts.statement: As of 31 January 2024, 3,604 Bangladeshis had set up a second home in Malaysia under the Malaysia My Second Home (MM2H) programme, fifth among nationalities; Bangladeshis were once third.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian Tourism, Arts and Culture Minister Datuk Seri Tiong King Sing in parliament, via Malay Mail

facts.statement: As of 31 January 2024 there were 56,066 active MM2H pass holders (participants and dependants): China 24,765, Australia 9,265, South Korea 4,940, Japan 4,733, Bangladesh 3,604, UK 2,234, and more than a thousand each from Taiwan, the US, Singapore and India.

In December 2023 Malaysia restructured MM2H into three tiers based on financial capacity: Platinum requires a fixed deposit of 5 million ringgit (50 lakh), Gold 2 million (20 lakh) and Silver 500,000 (5 lakh) ringgit; participants in all tiers must live in Malaysia a total of 60 days a year; applicants must be 30 or older. It was said the new scheme would run on trial for one year and be adjusted later.

Bangladesh Bank has so far allowed only a small number of companies to invest abroad; there are long-standing allegations that money laundered from Bangladesh funds 'second homes' in Canada and Malaysia, Singapore star hotels and Swiss bank deposits. An earlier government offer to bring laundered money back for a nominal tax was taken up by no one.

headline_en: Iftar of expatriate engineers and architects in Dubai
summary_en: The Dubai chapter of NRB Engineers and Architects, an association of Bangladeshi expatriate engineers and architects, held an iftar at Asia Royal restaurant in Dubai on Monday (about 25 March 2024), with Bangladesh's Consul General in Dubai and the Northern Emirates, B M Jamal Hossain, as chief guest. Chapters in Sharjah, Fujairah, Abu Dhabi and Al Ain were represented.

headline_en: Free internship in Japan for Bangladeshi undergraduate and postgraduate students
summary_en: Japan's Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) offers free 2-to-6-month research internships open to undergraduate and postgraduate students from any country, including Bangladesh, with a 15 April deadline. Interns get 2,400 yen per working day, visa support, air tickets, housing and insurance; the internship runs 1 October 2024 to 31 March 2025.

facts.statement: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST), Japan, offers free research internships of two to six months for undergraduate and postgraduate students from any country, including Bangladesh; application deadline 15 April (2024).

OIST research interns receive 2,400 Japanese yen per working day (the article converts this to BDT 1,840 at 0.77 taka per yen as of the afternoon of 3 January), plus free visa support, air tickets to and from Japan, housing and insurance.

OIST internship eligibility: students of any country at undergraduate or postgraduate level, with good results and good English. Required documents: a 400-word statement of purpose, academic mark sheets in English, copies of passport and national ID card, and a recommendation letter. Application is online.
OIST gives internships twice a year, selected on research topic, academic qualifications and merit; this round runs from 1 October 2024 to 31 March 2025.

headline_en: Oman migrant Bablu, who brought his family out of hardship, never made it home
summary_en: Md. Bablu (30) of Sonagazi, Feni, a supervisor at a company in Salalah, Oman for eight years, was killed in a road accident around midnight on Thursday (about 15 February 2024), a week before he was due home on 22 February; his family is worried about how to bring the body home and seeks government help. Separately, Mohammad Ali Sohag (30), also of Sonagazi, died on 9 February after falling from the roof of a 10-storey building under construction in Northern Cyprus; his body was brought home on 15 February and buried on 16 February.

facts.statement: Md. Bablu (30), son of Md. Selim of North Char Chandia village, Char Chandia union, Sonagazi upazila, Feni, was killed around 12 midnight on Thursday (about 15 February 2024) in Salalah, Oman, when the private car taking him from home to work was hit by another vehicle; several others with him were injured.

Md. Bablu went to Oman eight years earlier to support his poor family and worked as a supervisor at a company in Salalah; his income supported the family, paid for two sisters' weddings, and about eight months earlier he sent money from Oman to send his younger brother Md. Shiblu to Saudi Arabia. He was due to come home on 22 February 2024.

As of 16 February 2024, Bablu's family were worried about bringing his body home from Oman, did not know how to go about it and sought help from the government and others concerned; the Char Chandia union parishad chairman Md. Mosharraf Hossain said discussions were under way on how to bring the body home.
facts.source_in_article: uncle Motahar Hossain; UP chairman Md. Mosharraf Hossain

facts.statement: Bangladeshi youth Mohammad Ali Sohag (30), of Middle Char Chandia, Sonagazi, Feni, died on 9 February 2024 after falling from the roof of a 10-storey building under construction in Northern Cyprus.

Mohammad Ali Sohag's body was brought home from Northern Cyprus on Thursday night (15 February 2024) and buried in the family graveyard after a janaza at his home in Middle Char Chandia, Sonagazi at 10am on Friday 16 February 2024.
